title: use, re-exports, files and external crates
summary: Shorten paths with use, follow the idioms for what to import, rename with as, re-export with pub use, depend on external crates, and split a module tree across files.

blocks.md: Writing `crate::front_of_house::hosting::add_to_waitlist()` every time gets old fast. `use` creates a shortcut: a name in the current scope that stands for a path. It works like a symbolic link in a file system.

blocks.explain: A `use` only applies to the scope it is written in. If you moved `main` into a child module, the shortcut would not follow it: that module would need its own `use` (or `super::hosting`).

blocks.title: Idiomatic use paths
blocks.md:
Rust code follows two conventions, and following them makes code easier to read:

- For **functions**, bring the **parent module** into scope and call `hosting::add_to_waitlist()`. The module name shows the function is not defined locally.
- For **structs, enums and other types**, bring the **item itself** into scope: `use std::collections::HashMap;` then `HashMap::new()`.

The exception is two types with the same name from different modules. Then import the parent modules (`fmt::Result` and `io::Result`), or rename one with **`as`**:

blocks.title: Nested paths and globs
blocks.md:
Several imports from the same place can share a prefix in braces. `self` inside the braces imports the prefix itself:

```rust
use std::{cmp::Ordering, io};
use std::io::{self, Write};          // std::io and std::io::Write
use std::collections::*;             // every public item: use sparingly
```

The `*` **glob** brings everything public into scope. It makes it hard to tell where a name came from, so it is mostly used in tests (`use super::*;`, as in every exercise in this course) and for **preludes**: modules a library designs to be glob-imported.

blocks.title: The standard prelude
blocks.md: Why can you use `String`, `Vec`, `Option`, `Some` and `println!` without any `use`? Every module automatically imports the **standard prelude**, a short list of the most common items. Everything else in `std`, like `HashMap` or `io`, needs a `use`.

blocks.title: Re-exporting with pub use
blocks.md: A `use` is private by default: the shortcut works inside the module but is not part of its public API. `pub use` **re-exports** the name, so outside code can use the shorter path too. This lets you organize your code one way internally and present a simpler structure to users. Many crates re-export their most important types at the root: you write `use serde::Serialize`, not the deep path where it is defined.

blocks.title: External crates
blocks.md: In chapter 2 you added `rand` to `Cargo.toml` and wrote `use rand::prelude::*;`. That is all an external crate needs: a line under `[dependencies]` (or `cargo add rand`), then paths that start with the crate's name. Thousands of crates are published on [crates.io](https://crates.io). The standard library, `std`, is a crate too; it ships with Rust, so it never needs a `Cargo.toml` line, only `use` paths starting with `std`.

blocks.title: Splitting modules into files
blocks.md: As modules grow, move each into its own file. Replace the module's body with a semicolon, `mod front_of_house;`, and the compiler loads its contents from a file whose path follows the module tree:

blocks.title: Where the compiler looks for a module
rows: `src/tests.rs` (this is how every exercise in the course loads its tests)

blocks.title: The restaurant split across three files
blocks.explain: `mod` is a declaration, written **once** in the module tree, not an include. Other files refer to the module by path. An older layout, `src/front_of_house/mod.rs`, also works and is common in older code, but do not mix the two styles for the same module.

blocks.title: Tidy up with use
blocks.md: This program works but repeats long paths. Add `use` declarations at the top so that `main` can write `HashMap::new()`, `max(...)` and `geometry::area(...)`. Follow the idioms: import types directly, but import the **module** for your own function. The output must stay the same.
blocks.task: Make main use `HashMap::new()`, `max(a, b)` and `geometry::area(...)` with three use lines; the output must still be `largest: 12` and `area: 12` and `1 entry`.
hints: `use std::cmp::max;` is the usual exception for well-known standard functions; `use std::cmp;` then `cmp::max` is fine too.

questions.q: Which is the idiomatic way to call `add_to_waitlist` from `crate::front_of_house::hosting`?
questions.explanation: For functions, import the parent module so it is clear the function is not local.

questions.q: How do you import both `std::fmt::Result` and `std::io::Result`?
questions.explanation: Rename one with `as`, or import the parent modules and write `fmt::Result` and `io::Result`.

questions.q: What does `pub use crate::a::b::Thing;` at the crate root do?
options: Makes `Thing` public everywhere in the crate only
Re-exports `Thing` so users of the library can write `mycrate::Thing`
questions.explanation: A re-export adds the shorter path to the public API.

questions.q: In `src/lib.rs` you write `mod network;`. Where does the compiler look for its code?
questions.explanation: The file path follows the module path.

questions.q: `Vec` and `Option` need a `use` line before you can use them.
questions.explanation: They are in the standard prelude, imported automatically.

questions.q: `use std::io::{______, Write};` imports both `std::io` itself and `std::io::Write`.
questions.explanation: `self` in a nested path refers to the prefix.

points: `use path;` creates a shortcut in the current scope.
Idioms: import the parent module for functions, the item itself for types; rename clashes with `as`.
Nested paths `use std::{cmp::Ordering, io};` and `self` shorten import lists; globs `*` are for tests and preludes.
`pub use` re-exports, letting a library present a simpler public structure.
External crates: add to `[dependencies]`, then use paths starting with the crate name.
`mod name;` loads `name.rs` (or `name/mod.rs`); nested modules live in a folder named after the parent.

terms.def: A declaration that brings a path into scope under a short name.
Making an imported name part of your own public API with pub use.
use path::*; imports every public item from a module.
A set of items imported automatically; the standard prelude includes Option, Vec, String and more.
